lesson.title: Columbian Exchange
lesson.summary: How the transfer of diseases, crops, and animals between hemispheres after 1492 transformed populations, diets, and environments.
learningGoals: Explain the causes of the Columbian Exchange and its effects on the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
Explain how disease, crops, and animals changed populations and environments.
lesson.bigIdea: The Columbian Exchange reunited the biology of two hemispheres, causing a catastrophic population collapse in the Americas and new food supplies in Afro-Eurasia.
lesson.context: For thousands of years, the Americas and Afro-Eurasia had developed separate plants, animals, and diseases. After 1492, ships carried all three across the Atlantic.

sections.title: Disease and demographic collapse

blocks.text: Smallpox, measles, and influenza had no history in the Americas, so Indigenous people had no acquired immunity. A smallpox epidemic struck Tenochtitlan in 1520. Historians estimate that the Indigenous population of the Americas fell by as much as 90 percent within a century.
Disease combined with war, forced labor, and displacement. The collapse helped Spanish conquest and created labor shortages that colonists filled with enslaved Africans.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: New diseases killed huge numbers of Indigenous people, which weakened resistance to conquest and led colonists to import enslaved Africans to replace lost labor.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Disease was unintentional, but conquest, forced labor, and violence also caused deaths. A strong answer names both.

sections.takeaway: Epidemic disease was the deadliest part of the exchange and shaped the labor systems that followed.

sections.title: Crops and animals

blocks.text: Maize, potatoes, and manioc, first grown in the Americas, became staple foods across Europe, Africa, and Asia. Some historians link them to population growth in the 1700s.
Europeans brought wheat, sugarcane, horses, cattle, and pigs to the Americas. Horses changed hunting and warfare on the Great Plains, while grazing animals reshaped landscapes.

sections.takeaway: New foods fed growing populations in Afro-Eurasia, and new animals transformed American environments.

sections.title: Plantations and the environment

blocks.text: Sugarcane, originally from Asia, became the main plantation crop of Brazil and the Caribbean. Plantations cleared forests, exhausted soils, and relied on the forced labor of enslaved Africans.
Enslaved Africans also brought knowledge and crops, including rice cultivation in parts of the Americas. The exchange moved people and knowledge, not only plants and animals.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: The exchange was not equal. Indigenous Americans suffered population collapse, while Europeans gained land, crops, and wealth.

sections.takeaway: Plantation agriculture linked the Columbian Exchange to slavery and environmental change.

connections.title: Disease along trade routes
connections.body: The plague spread along Afro-Eurasian trade routes in the 1300s. After 1492, ships carried Afro-Eurasian diseases to the Americas with even more devastating results.
connections.transferQuestion: Compare the spread of the plague in the 1300s with the spread of smallpox after 1492.
connections.feedback: Name a similarity in how disease traveled and a difference in its effects.
